title: A contact path for a creative studio
metaTitle: Creative studio contact page: what happens next
excerpt: Say what happens after they reach out, how fast you really reply, and what to have ready. A ten-field form is how you lose the project.
alt: Two people pointing at a laptop screen, one wearing a fitness band, the kind of shared look a contact page should make easy to begin.

faqs.question: What should a contact page explain before the form?
faqs.answer: What happens next, who replies, how fast you actually respond, and the few things that make the reply useful. A URL, the job in a sentence, and a real timing are enough. The sequence should be visible without a manifesto.

faqs.question: How long can the form be?
faqs.answer: Keep it short: name, email, and the job cover the core, and each extra required field is a delay. Ask the rest in the reply, after you know the note is real. Ten fields is how serious buyers leave.

faqs.question: What counts as a reply?
faqs.answer: A sentence about their project, inside the window you published. An automatic note is not a reply. A calendar link with no context is not a reply. If you cannot keep the window, change the sentence on the page.

markdown:
A creative studio contact page should tell a client who has already seen fifty portfolios what happens after they reach out, how fast, and what to have ready. The action is to start a project. A form with ten fields is a way to lose them.

They already believe you might be able to choose, or they would not be here. The page has one job left: make the next step feel specific and light. Mystery is not professional. It reads as disorganized.

## What happens after they reach out

Write the sequence in three or four lines at the top, before the form. They send a note. You reply with a time or a few questions. You talk long enough to learn whether the project fits. If it fits, you send a scope. If it does not, you say so. A buyer should be able to picture the week after they press the button.

Name the thing the conversation is for. Fit, the shape of the work, and whether a proposal is worth writing. It is not a workshop, and it is not a free redesign. Saying that protects your time and calms a client who has been pulled into unpaid pitches by other studios. The client who has seen fifty portfolios has also seen fifty vague "discovery calls" that were sales theater. Tell them this one decides something.

Say who they will talk to. If the person on the call is the person who will do the work, say that. It matters to this buyer more than a brand film. If someone else joins for a store or for a brand system, say when. Do not promise "the founders" if a rotating inbox will answer.

Do not make them guess the channel. One path. A short form, or a booking link that still sits under the explanation. Two competing paths, a form and a calendar and an email and a chat widget, feel like a studio that has not decided how it works. Pick the path you will actually watch.

## How fast, stated so you can keep it

Publish a response window you have kept for the last month, not a slogan. "We reply within two working days" is a fact if it is true. "We reply instantly" is a mood, and it trains the wrong clients. Same-day is meaningful only if you mean same business day, and only if a person reads the note. An auto-reply is not a response. Say what the auto-reply is, if you send one, and what the human reply will add.

Be plain about weekends, holidays, and full weeks. A line that says you are booking intros for a later date is more trustworthy than a form that pretends the calendar is open. The buyer who is in a hurry can choose. The buyer who is not will respect the boundary. Fake availability is a small lie, and small lies are how a careful client predicts the project.

Do not publish a speed you only hit when the lead looks famous. The window is a standard or it is marketing. Standards go on this page. Marketing belongs in the work.

If you are often too busy to reply well, the page should say you are booking ahead, and the form should still be short. A long form in a busy week is worse, because you have asked them to work before you have the time to read it. Ask for less until you can respond to what you asked.

## What to have ready

Tell them the minimum that makes the reply useful. The URL of the current site, if there is one. The job in a sentence, such as a new marketing site, a store migration, or a product interface. The timing that is real. Anything that must not break. That is enough to know whether a conversation is worth it.

Optional, and labeled optional: a page they wish theirs resembled, and a page they know is wrong. References help. They are not a ticket you should refuse to read without. A client with a clear constraint and no deck is a better lead than a client with a forty-page brief and no decision.

Say what you do not need yet. A finished sitemap. A brand book. A budget written as a single number they are afraid to type. Account logins. The first conversation can happen without those. Asking for logins on a public form is a good way to be ignored, and it is careless.

Give them a sentence they can paste if they are stuck. "We need a site that shows one decision in the work and a way to start a project. Here is the current URL." A prompt like that lowers the cost of the blank box. People freeze on "Tell us about your project" because the box has no edges.

## Why ten fields lose the project

Each field is a question you are willing to delay the project to ask. Name, email, and the job in a sentence are the core. Company, and a rough timing, are reasonable. Budget can be a set of ranges if you will actually use it to judge fit, not as a trap. Phone number, job title, how they heard about you, company size, a file upload, a newsletter checkbox, and a terms essay are how a form becomes a CRM project.

[The W3C's WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) is the practical floor for whatever you keep. The form has to be understandable and operable. Every field needs a visible label, not only a placeholder that disappears when they type. Errors need to say what to fix. The button needs to say what it does. "Submit" is weaker than "Start a project." Contrast and focus have to work on a phone in daylight. A beautiful form that fails those basics will lose people for reasons you will misread as "low-quality leads."

Do not ask them to create an account. Do not gate the form behind a quiz that scores their brand maturity. Do not use a captcha that fails twice unless you have a real abuse problem. Friction should be spent on the conversation, not on the door.

If you need more detail, ask it in the reply, after you know the note is real. A second email with two questions feels attentive. A first form with fifteen required fields feels like a filter designed by someone who does not want to talk.

## The action is to start a project

Use the same words as the rest of the site. Start a project. Not "Submit inquiry," not "Let's collaborate," not "Send." The button is the last proof that one studio wrote the pages. A new verb on the last step suggests a new team.

Restate, under the button, what they will get. A reply inside the window you published. A conversation if there is a fit. A clear no if there is not. People press buttons when the result is described. They hesitate when the result is a void with a loading spinner.

After they send, the thank-you state has to continue the sequence. "We have it. We reply within two working days. If your timing is tighter, say so in a reply to the note." Do not dump them on a generic homepage. Do not start a newsletter sequence in the same breath. They came to start a project, not to join an audience.

Keep a human reachable if the form fails. A single email address in the footer is a reasonable backup, written as an address they can copy. Do not hide it in an image. Do not offer four addresses for new business, press, jobs, and hello if only one is watched. Watch the one you print.

## One owner

Someone has to own the inbox. If the form arrives in a channel nobody checks on a busy day, the page is fiction. Decide the owner, the backup, and what "replied" means. A reply is a sentence about their project, not a calendar link with no context, and not a PDF of your capabilities.

Record what they sent so the call does not make them repeat it. The URL, the job, the timing. The call can then spend its time on fit. That is the whole point of asking for those three things and not fifteen.

When the work starts, the contact page is no longer the home of the project. Notes, brand files, and updates should move to a place both sides can find. On a Hanabi project that place is the client portal. Your page does not need to explain the portal. It needs to avoid becoming a graveyard of attachments that should have lived somewhere calmer.

Read the page once a season against the last ten conversations. If you always ask a question the form did not, add it only if it changes whether you take the call. If you never use a field, delete it this week. The form should get shorter as you learn what a real lead looks like, not longer as tools make extra fields easy.

The contact page is also where leftover marketing tends to accumulate, because it feels safer than deleting it. A reel in the footer. A logo wall. A paragraph of praise. Cut those before they dilute the sequence. [What not to put on the site](/blog/what-not-to-put-on-the-site-for-a-creative-studio) is the next piece to write if the contact page, or any page, is still performing taste instead of telling the truth. A shorter page that says what happens next will outperform a long one that tries to close with atmosphere.

If you want to see whether your own first conversation is this clear, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the form you use today. The useful result is a shorter form, a window you can keep, and a sequence you could hand to a colleague without a meeting.
